title: Book 5, Chapter 17 — Sixteenth Year of the War—The Melian Conference—Fate of Melos
paragraphs: The next summer Alcibiades sailed with twenty ships to Argos and seized the suspected men still left of the Lacedaemonian faction, to the number of three hundred. The Athenians at once lodged them in the neighboring islands of their empire. The Athenians also made an expedition against the island of Melos with thirty ships of their own, six Chian and two Lesbian vessels, sixteen hundred heavy infantry, three hundred archers, and twenty mounted archers from Athens, and about fifteen hundred heavy infantry from the allies and the islanders. The Melians are a colony of Lacedaemon and refused to submit to the Athenians like the other islanders. At first they remained neutral and took no part in the struggle. But afterwards, when the Athenians used violence and plundered their territory, they took up an attitude of open hostility. Cleomedes, son of Lycomedes, and Tisias, son of Tisimachus, the generals, encamping in their territory with the above force, before doing any damage to their land, sent envoys to negotiate. The Melians did not bring them before the people, but told them to state the object of their mission to the magistrates and the few. The Athenian envoys then spoke as follows:

Athenians. Since the negotiations are not to go on before the people — so that we may not be able to speak straight through without interruption and deceive the ears of the multitude with seductive arguments that would pass without refutation (for we know this is the meaning of our being brought before the few) — what if you who sit there were to pursue a method even more cautious still? Make no set speech yourselves, but take us up at whatever you do not like, and settle that before going any further. And first tell us whether this proposal of ours suits you.
The Melian commissioners answered:

Melians. To the fairness of quietly instructing one another as you propose there is nothing to object. But your military preparations are too far advanced to agree with what you say. We see that you have come to be judges in your own cause, and that all we can reasonably expect from this negotiation is war, if we prove to have right on our side and refuse to submit, and in the contrary case, slavery.

Athenians. If you have come to reason about presentiments of the future, or for anything other than to consult about the safety of your state on the facts you see before you, we will give it up. Otherwise we will go on.

Melians. It is natural and excusable for men in our position to turn more ways than one in both thought and speech. However, the question at this conference is, as you say, the safety of our country, and the discussion, if you please, may proceed in the way you propose.

Athenians. We for our part will not trouble you with specious pretexts — either that we have a right to our empire because we overthrew the Mede, or that we are now attacking you for wrong you have done us — and make a long speech that would not be believed. In return we hope that you, instead of thinking to influence us by saying that you did not join the Lacedaemonians, although their colonists, or that you have done us no wrong, will aim at what is feasible, keeping in view the real sentiments of us both. For you know as well as we do that, as the world goes, right is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

Melians. In our view, at any rate, it is expedient — we speak as we are forced to, since you tell us to set right aside and talk only of interest — that you should not destroy what is our common protection: the privilege of being allowed in danger to invoke what is fair and right, and even to profit by arguments not strictly valid if they can be made to pass. And you are as much interested in this as any, since your own fall would be the signal for the heaviest vengeance and would set an example for the world to ponder.

Athenians. The end of our empire, if end it must, does not frighten us. A rival empire like Lacedaemon, even if Lacedaemon were our real antagonist, is not so terrible to the vanquished as subjects who attack and overpower their rulers on their own. This, however, is a risk we are content to run. We will now proceed to show you that we have come here in the interest of our empire, and that we shall say what we are now going to say, for the preservation of your country. We would gladly exercise that empire over you without trouble, and see you preserved for the good of us both.
Melians. And how, pray, could it turn out as good for us to serve as it is for you to rule?
Athenians. Because you would have the advantage of submitting before suffering the worst, and we should gain by not destroying you.
Melians. So you would not agree to our being neutral, friends instead of enemies, but allies of neither side?
Athenians. No. Your hostility does not hurt us as much as your friendship would; for friendship would be an argument to our subjects of our weakness, while your enmity is proof of our power.

Melians. Is that what your subjects regard as fair, that you should put those who have nothing to do with you in the same category as peoples who are mostly your own colonists, and some of them conquered rebels?

Athenians. As far as right goes, they think one has as much of it as the other, and that if any maintain their independence it is because they are strong, and that if we do not interfere with them it is because we are afraid. So besides extending our empire, we would gain in security by your subjection — and the fact that you are islanders and weaker than others makes it all the more important that you should not succeed in defying the masters of the sea.

Melians. But do you consider there is no security in the policy we indicate? For here again, if you bar us from talking about justice and invite us to obey your interest, we also must explain ours, and try to persuade you if the two happen to coincide. How can you avoid making enemies of all existing neutrals, who will conclude from your example that one day or another you will attack them? What is this but to multiply the enemies you already have, and to force others to become so who would otherwise never have thought of it?

Athenians. The fact is that continentals generally give us little alarm. The liberty they enjoy will long prevent their taking precautions against us. It is rather islanders like yourselves, outside our empire, and subjects smarting under the yoke, who would be the most likely to take a rash step and lead themselves and us into obvious danger.

Melians. Well then, if you risk so much to retain your empire, and your subjects to get rid of it, it would surely be great baseness and cowardice in us, who are still free, not to try everything that can be tried before submitting to your yoke.

Athenians. Not if you are well advised. The contest is not an equal one, with honor as the prize and shame as the penalty; it is a question of self-preservation, of not resisting those who are far stronger than you are.

Melians. But we know that the fortune of war is sometimes more impartial than the disproportion of numbers might lead one to suppose. To submit is to give ourselves over to despair, while action still preserves the hope that we may yet stand erect.

Athenians. Hope, danger's comforter, may be indulged in by those who have abundant resources — if not without loss, at least without ruin. But its nature is to be extravagant, and those who go so far as to stake their all on it see it in its true colors only when they are ruined. So long as the discovery would enable them to guard against it, hope is never found wanting. Let this not be the case with you, who are weak and hang on a single turn of the scale. Do not be like the vulgar, who, abandoning such security as human means may still afford when visible hopes fail them in extremity, turn to the invisible — to prophecies, oracles, and other such inventions that delude men with hopes to their destruction.

Melians. You may be sure that we are as well aware as you of the difficulty of contending against your power and your fortune unless the terms be equal. Still, we trust that the gods may grant us fortune as good as yours, since we are just men fighting against unjust men, and that what we lack in power will be made up by the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, who are bound, if only out of shame, to come to the aid of their kindred. Our confidence, after all, is therefore not so utterly irrational.

Athenians. When you speak of the favor of the gods, we may as fairly hope for that as you. Neither our pretensions nor our conduct is in any way contrary to what men believe of the gods or practice among themselves. Of the gods we believe, and of men we know, that by a necessary law of their nature they rule wherever they can. We did not make this law, nor were we the first to act on it once it was made. We found it existing before us and shall leave it to exist forever after us. All we are doing is making use of it, knowing that you, and everyone else with the same power as we have, would do the same as we do. Thus, as far as the gods are concerned, we have no fear and no reason to fear that we shall be at a disadvantage. But when we come to your notion about the Lacedaemonians, which makes you believe that shame will make them help you, here we admire your simplicity but do not envy your folly. The Lacedaemonians, when their own interests or their country's laws are at stake, are the worthiest men alive. As to their conduct toward others, much could be said, but no clearer idea of it could be given than by saying briefly that, of all the men we know, they are the most conspicuous in considering what is agreeable to be honorable, and what is expedient to be just. Such a way of thinking does not promise much for the safety which you now unreasonably count on.

Melians. But it is for this very reason that we now trust to their concern for expediency to keep them from betraying the Melians, their colonists, and so losing the confidence of their friends in Hellas and helping their enemies.

Athenians. So you do not adopt the view that expediency goes with security, while justice and honor cannot be followed without danger — and the Lacedaemonians as a rule court danger as little as possible.

Melians. But we believe that they would be more likely to face even danger for our sake, and with more confidence than for others, since our nearness to the Peloponnese makes it easier for them to act, and our common blood is a guarantee of our fidelity.

Athenians. Yes, but what an intending ally trusts to is not the goodwill of those who ask his help, but a decided superiority of power for action — and the Lacedaemonians look to this even more than others do. At any rate, their distrust of their home resources is such that it is only with numerous allies that they attack a neighbor. Is it likely, then, that while we are masters of the sea they will cross over to an island?

Melians. But they would have others to send. The Cretan Sea is wide, and it is harder for those who command it to intercept others than for those who wish to slip past them to do so safely. And if the Lacedaemonians failed in this, they would fall on your land, and on those of your allies left untouched by Brasidas. Instead of places that are not yours, you would have to fight for your own country and your own confederacy.

Athenians. Some such diversion as you speak of you may one day experience, only to learn — as others have learned — that the Athenians never once yet withdrew from a siege out of fear of anyone. But we are struck by the fact that, after saying you would consult about the safety of your country, in all this discussion you have mentioned nothing that men might trust in and think to be saved by. Your strongest arguments depend on hope and the future, and your actual resources are too scant compared with those arrayed against you for you to come out victorious. You will therefore show great blindness of judgment unless, after allowing us to retire, you can find some plan more prudent than this. You will surely not be caught by that idea of disgrace which, in dangers that are disgraceful and at the same time too plain to be mistaken, proves so ruinous to mankind. In all too many cases the very men whose eyes are perfectly open to what they are rushing into still let the thing called disgrace, by the mere force of a seductive name, lead them on to a point where they become so enslaved by the phrase that they wilfully fall into hopeless disaster, and incur a disgrace all the more disgraceful for being the companion of error rather than the result of misfortune. If you are well advised, you will guard against this. You will not think it dishonorable to submit to the greatest city in Hellas, when it makes you the moderate offer of becoming its tributary ally without ceasing to enjoy the country that belongs to you. Nor, when you are given the choice between war and security, will you be so blinded as to choose the worse. And it is certain that those who do not yield to their equals, who keep terms with their superiors, and are moderate toward their inferiors, on the whole succeed best. Think the matter over, then, after our withdrawal. Reflect again and again that it is your country you are deliberating about, that you have only one, and that on this single deliberation depends its prosperity or its ruin.

The Athenians now withdrew from the conference, and the Melians, left to themselves, came to a decision corresponding to what they had maintained in the discussion, and answered: "Our resolution, Athenians, is the same as it was at first. We will not in a moment deprive of freedom a city that has been inhabited these seven hundred years. We put our trust in the fortune by which the gods have preserved it until now, and in the help of men — that is, of the Lacedaemonians — and so we will try to save ourselves. Meanwhile we invite you to allow us to be friends to you and foes to neither party, and to withdraw from our country after making such a treaty as shall seem fit to us both."

Such was the answer of the Melians. The Athenians, leaving the conference, said: "Well, you alone, judging from these resolutions, seem to us to regard what is future as more certain than what is before your eyes, and what is out of sight, in your eagerness, as already coming to pass. As you have staked most on, and trusted most in, the Lacedaemonians, your fortune, and your hopes, so will you be most completely deceived."

The Athenian envoys now returned to the army. The Melians showing no signs of yielding, the generals at once turned to hostilities and drew a line of circumvallation around Melos, dividing the work among the various states. The Athenians then went back with most of their army, leaving behind a certain number of their own citizens and of the allies to keep guard by land and sea. The force thus left stayed on and besieged the place.

About the same time the Argives invaded the territory of Phlius and lost eighty men cut off in an ambush by the Phliasians and Argive exiles. Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos took so much plunder from the Lacedaemonians that the latter, although they still refrained from breaking off the treaty and going to war with Athens, proclaimed that any of their people who chose might plunder the Athenians. The Corinthians also began hostilities with the Athenians, over private quarrels of their own. But the rest of the Peloponnesians stayed quiet. Meanwhile the Melians attacked by night and took the part of the Athenian lines opposite the market, killed some of the men, and brought in corn and everything else they could find useful, and then withdrew and kept quiet. The Athenians took measures to keep better watch in future.

Summer was now over. The following winter the Lacedaemonians intended to invade Argive territory, but on reaching the frontier they found the sacrifices for crossing unfavorable and went back again. This intention of theirs gave the Argives suspicions of certain of their fellow citizens, some of whom they arrested, though others escaped them. About the same time the Melians again took another part of the Athenian lines, which were only feebly garrisoned. When reinforcements arrived from Athens in consequence, under the command of Philocrates son of Demeas, the siege was now pressed vigorously. With some treachery occurring inside, the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men they took, and sold the women and children as slaves. They afterwards sent out five hundred colonists and settled the place themselves.
